newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean military on standby to ease strike damage.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean military on standby to ease strike damage.

text.p: South Korea's military was on standby on Monday to keep trains and telephone services running as militant unions went ahead with plans for the biggest strike in the country's history.
Media reports said a force of 2,500 specialists had been trained to take over from railway drivers and telecommunications workers.
"If anything happens, the military will be mobilised," a defence ministry spokesman said.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions has called out its 1.2 million members on Tuesday for a two-day strike to try to force the government to dump a new labour law.

They will be joined on Wednesday by members of the 500,000-strong Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has vowed an indefinite walkout against the bill that allows worker layoffs -- almost unheard of in South Korea.
On Monday the chairman of the ruling New Korea party made a dramatic visit to a Seoul cathedral where confederation leaders are sheltering from arrest for organising wildcat strikes.
But Lee Hong-koo, who has tried to end three weeks of industrial unrest with appeals for dialogue, was turned away by blue-collar workers acting as bodyguards for leaders of the outlawed union body.
Instead, he met the Roman Catholic cardinal of South Korea and was lectured by him on worker welfare.
"Get out, get out", workers chanted as Lee's limousine pulled up outside Myongdong Cathedral, where union leaders are holed up in a ramshackle tent.
A union official said strike leaders would only meet Lee if the government revoked the labour law and withdrew arrest warrants against them.

The law, which the government says is needed to make the labour market more flexible and lower industrial costs, also allows employers to replace strikers and delays official recognition of the confederation until 2000.
Official figures showed production losses from strikes after the labour bill was rammed through parliament on december 26 would cost the country 1.96 trillion won ($2.3 billion) by the end of Monday.
Lee skirted close to the strike tent on his way to a cathedral building for his meeting with Cardinal Kim Soo-hwan.
"I'm sorry and embarrassed for causing you trouble," Lee told the spirtual head of the country's 3.5 million Roman Catholics.

The cardinal replied: "I understand you have passed a law to save the economy, but I hope we all understand that to love this country we have to increase the quality of life for workers as well as save the economy".
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung was uncompromising, warning the Myongdong unionists they could not evade the law forever, according to Yonhap news agency.

Lee said police would refrain from making arrests "out of respect for freedom of religion and the church's dignity", but eventually there would be a reckoning, Yonhap reported, without saying where Lee made his comments.
Lee said the government should be fully prepared to minimise disruption if subways and telecommunications were hit by strikes.
Buoyant strike leaders, claiming public opinion was on their side, are plotting to idle key parts of South Korea's usually roaring export machine.
Their stepped-up actions starting on Tuesday is also designed to cause massive disruption to public services that have so far largely escaped unscathed.

Hospital workers have staged intermittent strikes that briefly closed out-patient care in leading medical centres, but previous subway driver stoppages failed miserably after non-union workers stepped in.

Federation leaders have urged power, port and railway workers to go on partial strike and all others to join a total shutdown on Tuesday. Buses, subways, hospitals, banks, hotels, taxis, newspapers and state industries will be hit.
The confederation controls union workers at state telecommunications giant Korea Telecom and at the giant Hyundai and Daewoo groups.
